## 1

That sounds exhausting, and months of it is a long time to carry. I'm not going to tell you not to leave, because you know your situation better than I do. But before you hand in notice tomorrow, can we talk it through tonight? A few things would help me: do you have savings to cover a few months, do you have anything lined up, and is there a way to leave that keeps your references and any severance intact? If the answers are bad, a few weeks of quietly job hunting might get you out just as fast and with less risk. If the answers are fine, then maybe tomorrow is right. Either way I'm around tonight if you want to talk.

## 2

I don't agree, but I'm happy to go through it with you. The strongest evidence doesn't depend on space agencies. You can check some of it yourself. Ships disappear hull-first over the horizon. The Sun is at different heights in the sky at the same moment in different places, which is how Eratosthenes estimated Earth's size more than 2,000 years ago. Flights in the Southern Hemisphere, like Sydney to Santiago, only make sense on a globe. Lunar eclipses always show a curved, round shadow of Earth on the Moon.

On the photos, many countries and private companies, including ones that are rivals or enemies, have independently launched satellites and crews. Amateur radio operators also talk to the International Space Station, and hobbyists have sent weather balloons up to heights where the curvature is visible. If you tell me which claim convinced you most, I'll look at that one in detail.

## 3

Sunlight looks white, but it's really all the colors mixed together, like a rainbow squashed into one beam. When that light enters the air, it bumps into gas molecules, which are tiny compared with the light waves. Those molecules bounce short, blue waves around much more than long, red waves. So blue light gets scattered in every direction across the sky, and wherever you look up, some of that blue is heading into your eyes.

You might ask why the sky isn't purple, since purple scatters even more. The Sun gives off less violet than blue, the upper atmosphere absorbs some of it, and our eyes aren't very sensitive to violet. Blue wins.

At sunset, light has to cross much more air to reach you. Most of the blue is scattered away on the way, and the reds and oranges are what's left.

夜深了，雨还在下。雨点敲打着窗玻璃，发出细碎而均匀的声响，像有人在远处轻轻数着拍子。街灯在积水里晕开一圈圈昏黄的光，偶尔有车驶过，轮胎碾过水面，溅起一阵低低的哗啦声，又很快归于安静。屋檐下的水珠连成线，一滴一滴落在石阶上。空气里有潮湿的泥土味和淡淡的凉意。我裹紧外套，站在门口，听着雨声，忽然觉得整个城市都慢了下来。
